title: Your neighbor
hook: faith lived beside neighbors of every kind

segments.voice: Yesterday: your family, service at home, then the prayer, and patience above all. Your line was pray together.

The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, once told his companions: Jibril kept urging me to treat the neighbor well, so often that I thought he was going to make the neighbor an heir. That report is in Sahih al-Bukhari. An heir. Someone with a share in what is yours, written into the family accounts. The person whose music comes through the wall, whose car blocks yours, whose name you might not even know. You met the neighbor back on day one hundred fifty-four. Today, faith lived beside neighbors of every kind.
screen: `JIBRIL KEPT URGING.` → `AS IF THE NEIGHBOR WERE AN HEIR.` → `THE ONE THROUGH THE WALL.`

segments.voice: In surah an-Nisa, in a list of those to be treated with kindness, after parents, relatives, orphans and the needy, the Qur'an names the neighbor who is related to you, the neighbor who is a stranger, and the companion at your side. Two kinds of neighbor in one verse: one who shares your family, and one who shares nothing with you but a fence. The bar is set high. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet says: whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honor his neighbor. And in the same collection, that a person whose neighbor isn't safe from his harm will not enter paradise. So a neighbor isn't a matter of manners. It sits right next to faith itself. Neighbors of every kind, too. A report in the collections of Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi tells of the companion Abdullah ibn Amr, who had a sheep slaughtered at home and asked his household: have you given some to our Jewish neighbor? Then he repeated the hadith of Jibril and the neighbor. The neighbor's faith didn't change the neighbor's right. On an ordinary street it starts small. Knowing a name. Not letting your trash cans block a driveway. Keeping the noise down at night. A plate of food over the fence on a holiday, any holiday. Checking on the older man upstairs when it snows. Rights like these are small, and they're owed whether or not the neighbor returns them.
screen: `THE NEAR NEIGHBOR AND THE STRANGER.` · `HONOR YOUR NEIGHBOR.` · `HAVE YOU GIVEN SOME NEXT DOOR?` · `SMALL RIGHTS, OWED ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: In your mind, step out your front door and look left, right, up or down, silently naming every neighbor whose name you know, and notice where the names run out. Pick one door where you don't know a name, and let one small, easy reason to knock come to mind: an introduction, a plate of something, a question about the building. If you pray, ask Allah to bless the people on your street.
Your neighbor. The person on the other side of the wall, whose rights the Qur'an and the Prophet set right next to faith. Today's word.
Your line: start next door. A name is where it begins. Day one thousand four hundred nine, done.

howItsDone: Muslims treat the neighbor's rights as part of faith, following the Qur'an's command to be kind to the near and the stranger neighbor and the hadith 'let him honor his neighbor'; this can mean sharing food on holidays, avoiding noise and harm, and checking on neighbors of any faith.

what it means: someone with real rights over you, whatever their faith, starting with a name, a plate of food and no harm.
what a scholar hears: an-Nisa's near neighbor and stranger neighbor, Jibril urging until the neighbor seemed an heir, and Abdullah ibn Amr's question about his Jewish neighbor.

chat.says: Does Islam ask Muslims to treat non-Muslim neighbors well too?
options: Yes. A companion made sure his Jewish neighbor got a share; faith doesn't change the right.
Only if the neighbor is a relative; strangers next door have no real claim.
Only as good manners; the hadith doesn't link neighbors to faith at all.
chat.meaning: The Qur'an names the neighbor who is a stranger, and Abdullah ibn Amr asked: have you given some to our Jewish neighbor? Faith didn't change the right.

notes: Confirm Sahih al-Bukhari 6014 (Jibril and the neighbor as heir), Sahih Muslim 47 (let him honor his neighbor) and Sahih Muslim 46 (whose neighbor is not safe from his harm).
Qur'an 4:36 is paraphrased; check the rendering of 'the neighbor who is related', 'the neighbor who is a stranger' and 'the companion at your side'.
Check the Abdullah ibn Amr report (Abu Dawud 5152; Tirmidhi 1943), its grading.
The everyday examples (trash cans, noise, food on a holiday, checking on an older neighbor) are illustrations, not sourced rulings.
